research_text:
## Factual research brief

### 1. What `javax.crypto.SecretKeyFactory` governs, and what the finding refers to

`javax.crypto.SecretKeyFactory` is the JCA factory for **secret (symmetric) keys**. Its documented role is conversion between opaque `SecretKey` objects and transparent `KeySpec` representations: `generateSecret(KeySpec)` creates a secret key from a specification, while `getKeySpec` obtains a representation of a key. Supported `KeySpec` types are provider-specific.  
Direct source: https://docs.oracle.com/en/java/javase/25/docs/api/java.base/javax/crypto/SecretKeyFactory.html ([docs.oracle.com](https://docs.oracle.com/en/java/javase/25/docs/api/java.base/javax/crypto/SecretKeyFactory.html))

For the reported rule, the value at issue is specifically the **`algorithm` string supplied to `SecretKeyFactory.getInstance`**:

* `getInstance(algorithm)`; or
* `getInstance(algorithm, _)`.

Thus, “found `PBKDF2WithHmacSHA1`” refers to the factory algorithm-name argument, not to a `PBEKeySpec` field, salt, iteration count, key length, ciphertext format, or a call to `generateSecret`. The rule’s explicit membership constraint excludes `PBKDF2WithHmacSHA1`, so that string does not satisfy the rule’s stated allowlist. ([raw.githubusercontent.com](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/CROSSINGTUD/Crypto-API-Rules/refs/heads/master/JavaCryptographicArchitecture/src/SecretKeyFactory.crysl))

That is a rule-specific conclusion, not an assertion that the Java API rejects the string. Oracle’s JDK 25 SunJCE provider documentation lists `PBKDF2WithHmacSHA1` among supported `SecretKeyFactory` algorithms, alongside SHA-2 PBKDF2 variants.  
Direct source: https://docs.oracle.com/en/java/javase/25/security/oracle-providers.html ([docs.oracle.com](https://docs.oracle.com/en/java/javase/25/security/oracle-providers.html))

---

### 2. Documented correct/safe API usage and documented remediation

#### Documented API usage

The Java API documents these relevant requirements and behaviors:

* `getInstance` accepts the **standard name** of the requested secret-key algorithm and selects an implementation from registered providers; an unavailable algorithm produces `NoSuchAlgorithmException`. The overloads accepting a provider restrict lookup to that provider. ([docs.oracle.com](https://docs.oracle.com/en/java/javase/25/docs/api/java.base/javax/crypto/SecretKeyFactory.html))
* Java’s standard-name specification describes `PBKDF2With<prf>` as a PBKDF2 password-based key-derivation algorithm using the chosen PRF, with `PBKDF2WithHmacSHA256` as an example. It similarly describes `PBEWith<prf>And<encryption>` as a PKCS #5 password-based-encryption factory name. Standard names are documented as **not case-sensitive**.  
  Direct source: https://docs.oracle.com/en/java/javase/25/docs/specs/security/standard-names.html ([docs.oracle.com](https://docs.oracle.com/en/java/javase/25/docs/specs/security/standard-names.html))
* For password-based uses, `PBEKeySpec` documents use of a `char[]` rather than a `String` so password material can be overwritten, and provides `clearPassword()`. Its salt-taking constructors reject a null or empty salt and non-positive iteration count; it does not set an application-specific security strength target.  
  Direct source: https://docs.oracle.com/en/java/javase/25/docs/api/java.base/javax/crypto/spec/PBEKeySpec.html ([docs.oracle.com](https://docs.oracle.com/en/java/javase/25/docs/api/java.base/javax/crypto/spec/PBEKeySpec.html))
* Oracle’s provider guidance says general-purpose applications should normally use the no-provider `getInstance("...")` form rather than pinning a provider, because pinning harms portability and can bypass higher-priority optimized implementations. This is provider-selection guidance, not an algorithm-selection recommendation.  
  Direct source: https://docs.oracle.com/en/java/javase/25/security/oracle-providers.html ([docs.oracle.com](https://docs.oracle.com/en/java/javase/25/security/oracle-providers.html))

For PBKDF2 used to derive keys from passwords for stored-data applications, NIST SP 800-132 specifies use of an approved random-generated salt portion of at least 128 bits, an iteration count as large as practical for the application, and a derived-key length of at least 112 bits. It approves PBKDF2 with HMAC using an approved hash function. This is a 2010 NIST storage-applications document, so it is not evidence of a current application-specific policy or of the detector’s intended policy.  
Direct source: https://nvlpubs.nist.gov/nistpubs/Legacy/SP/nistspecialpublication800-132.pdf ([nvlpubs.nist.gov](https://nvlpubs.nist.gov/nistpubs/Legacy/SP/nistspecialpublication800-132.pdf))

#### Documented remediation

The `SecretKeyFactory` API documentation does **not** prescribe a remediation of the form “replace `PBKDF2WithHmacSHA1` with one of these twelve names.” Nor does it define the rule’s allowlist as a Java-platform safe-algorithm policy. In fact, the current Oracle SunJCE documentation lists `PBKDF2WithHmacSHA1` as supported. ([docs.oracle.com](https://docs.oracle.com/en/java/javase/25/security/oracle-providers.html))

The only directly relevant documented remediation-like guidance found is:

1. avoid specifying a named provider in general-purpose applications where portability is desired; and
2. consult the selected provider’s documentation for supported `KeySpec` types and algorithms. ([docs.oracle.com](https://docs.oracle.com/en/java/javase/25/docs/api/java.base/javax/crypto/SecretKeyFactory.html))

Accordingly, official `SecretKeyFactory` documentation alone does not establish a specific replacement algorithm or a complete migration prescription for this finding. The detector’s security-policy rationale and the intended target runtime/provider remain unresolved by those API sources.

---

### 3. Compatibility: persisted data, wire formats, platform support, and migration

#### Persisted and wire formats

`SecretKeyFactory` itself specifies no persistence format, wire format, serialized representation, or data-migration mechanism. It creates/translates key objects and key specifications; the key-spec support and implementation are provider-dependent. ([docs.oracle.com](https://docs.oracle.com/en/java/javase/25/docs/api/java.base/javax/crypto/SecretKeyFactory.html))

For **standardized PKCS #5 PBKDF2/PBES2 encodings**, RFC 8018 defines `PBKDF2-params` containing salt, iteration count, optional key length, and a PRF `AlgorithmIdentifier`; the default PRF is HMAC-SHA-1 if the PRF field is omitted. It also defines PBES2 parameters as a key-derivation-function identifier plus an encryption-scheme identifier. The RFC states that salt, iteration count, key length, and identifiers for the KDF and encryption scheme may be conveyed in an `AlgorithmIdentifier`.  
Direct source: https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc8018.html ([rfc-editor.org](https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc8018.html))

Therefore, for a PKCS #5/PBES2-formatted value, the PRF/KDF choice is protocol-relevant metadata. As an inference from the specified PBKDF2 parameters, a consumer must use the recorded—or, when omitted, defaulted—PRF to reproduce the specified derivation. This does **not** establish what any local persisted format contains, because that is outside the Java API and was not supplied.

Neither `SecretKeyFactory` nor RFC 8018 provides a general, Java-specific migration path from one PBKDF2 PRF name to another. RFC 8018 describes parameter encoding and encryption/decryption operations, not an application data-transition procedure. ([rfc-editor.org](https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc8018.html))

#### Platform-version and provider support

Availability is not portable merely because an algorithm name is standard. The Java API says every implementation must support `DESede` for `SecretKeyFactory` and directs users to release/provider documentation for other supported algorithms. ([docs.oracle.com](https://docs.oracle.com/en/java/javase/25/docs/api/java.base/javax/crypto/SecretKeyFactory.html))

The Oracle provider documents show version-dependent bundled-provider support:

* The Java SE 7 SunJCE list includes `PBKDF2WithHmacSHA1` but does not list the SHA-224/SHA-256/SHA-384/SHA-512 PBKDF2 factory variants.  
  Direct source: https://docs.oracle.com/javase/7/docs/technotes/guides/security/SunProviders.html ([docs.oracle.com](https://docs.oracle.com/javase/7/docs/technotes/guides/security/SunProviders.html))
* The JDK 8 SunJCE list includes `PBKDF2WithHmacSHA1`, `PBKDF2WithHmacSHA224`, `PBKDF2WithHmacSHA256`, `PBKDF2WithHmacSHA384`, and `PBKDF2WithHmacSHA512`.  
  Direct source: https://docs.oracle.com/javase/8/docs/technotes/guides/security/SunProviders.html ([docs.oracle.com](https://docs.oracle.com/javase/8/docs/technotes/guides/security/SunProviders.html))
* The current JDK 25 SunJCE list includes those algorithms and additional SHA-512 truncated variants. ([docs.oracle.com](https://docs.oracle.com/en/java/javase/25/security/oracle-providers.html))

These sources document Oracle-provided SunJCE behavior for those documented platform versions; they do not establish availability in every JVM distribution, in every update level, or through every third-party/provider configuration.

---

### 4. Exact `Crypto-API-Rules` matching rule

Source: https://raw.githubusercontent.com/CROSSINGTUD/Crypto-API-Rules/refs/heads/master/JavaCryptographicArchitecture/src/SecretKeyFactory.crysl

The rule’s type declaration and event clauses state, verbatim:

```text
SPEC javax.crypto.SecretKeyFactory

OBJECTS
    java.lang.String algorithm;
    javax.crypto.SecretKey key;
    javax.crypto.SecretKey otherKey;
    java.security.spec.KeySpec keySpec;

EVENTS
    g1: getInstance(algorithm);
    g2: getInstance(algorithm, _);
    Get := g1 | g2;

    gS: key = generateSecret(keySpec);
    tK: key = translateKey(otherKey);
    Gen := gS | tK;
```

It then states:

```text
ORDER
    Get, Gen
CONSTRAINTS
    algorithm in {"PBKDF2WithHmacSHA512", "PBKDF2WithHmacSHA384", "PBKDF2WithHmacSHA256", "PBKDF2WithHmacSHA224",
                "PBEWithHmacSHA512AndAES_128","PBEWithHmacSHA384AndAES_128", "PBEWithHmacSHA384AndAES_128",
                "PBEWithHmacSHA224AndAES_128", "PBEWithHmacSHA256AndAES_128","PBEWithHmacSHA224AndAES_256",
                "PBEWithHmacSHA256AndAES_256", "PBEWithHmacSHA384AndAES_256", "PBEWithHmacSHA512AndAES_256"};

REQUIRES
    speccedKey[keySpec, _];

ENSURES
    generatedKey[key, algorithm];
```

([raw.githubusercontent.com](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/CROSSINGTUD/Crypto-API-Rules/refs/heads/master/JavaCryptographicArchitecture/src/SecretKeyFactory.crysl))

#### What it matches and constrains

| Rule event | Declared API method | Declared arguments/results | Constraint in this file |
|---|---|---|---|
| `g1` | `getInstance` | One argument: `algorithm` | `algorithm` must be a member of the listed string set. |
| `g2` | `getInstance` | Two arguments: `algorithm, _` | The first argument is constrained by the same set; `_` is not constrained in this file. |
| `gS` | `generateSecret` | `key = generateSecret(keySpec)` | Requires `speccedKey[keySpec, _]`; ensures `generatedKey[key, algorithm]`. |
| `tK` | `translateKey` | `key = translateKey(otherKey)` | Ensures `generatedKey[key, algorithm]`; no event-specific `REQUIRES` predicate for `otherKey` is written. |

The declared receiver/API type is `javax.crypto.SecretKeyFactory`, through `SPEC javax.crypto.SecretKeyFactory`. The source has no event for `getKeySpec`, and its method-event declarations do not include arbitrary methods with the same names.

**Can it match a method that merely shares an API method name?** **The rule text does not declare a name-only matcher.** It declares a specification for `javax.crypto.SecretKeyFactory`; no clause states that any unrelated method called `getInstance`, `generateSecret`, or `translateKey` matches. However, this `.crysl` file does not document the analyzer’s dispatch/type-resolution implementation. Therefore, from this source alone, it is not possible to independently verify the analyzer’s operational behavior for unresolved calls, erroneous type resolution, wrappers, or methods sharing a name. ([raw.githubusercontent.com](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/CROSSINGTUD/Crypto-API-Rules/refs/heads/master/JavaCryptographicArchitecture/src/SecretKeyFactory.crysl))

### Source limitations and unresolved questions

* The CRYSL source defines the literal allowlist and event protocol, but not why that particular security policy was selected.
* It leaves `speccedKey[keySpec, _]` undefined; this file does not identify which other rule produces it.
* It does not specify detector handling for aliases, capitalization normalization, exceptions, reachability, provider availability, or unresolved dispatch. This matters because Java’s standard-name documentation says standard names are not case-sensitive, while the CRYSL condition is expressed as capitalized string literals. ([docs.oracle.com](https://docs.oracle.com/en/java/javase/25/docs/specs/security/standard-names.html))
* No repository-specific call site, data format, runtime version, provider configuration, or interoperability requirement was supplied. Those facts are necessary to determine compatibility consequences or a migration path.
